title: Friends of the Earth, Inc. v. Laidlaw Environmental Services (TOC), Inc.
lead: River users sue over continuing permit violations, but their penalty would go to the Treasury. Later compliance and closure require the courts to distinguish standing at filing from a case becoming moot.

actors.name: Friends of the Earth, Citizens Local Environmental Action Network, and Sierra Club
actors.role: Environmental citizen-plaintiffs asserting injuries to their members.

actors.name: Laidlaw Environmental Services (TOC), Inc.
actors.role: Operator of a South Carolina wastewater-treatment facility discharging to the North Tyger River.

actors.name: South Carolina DHEC
actors.role: State environmental agency that sued and settled with Laidlaw before the citizen complaint.

proceedings: The district court allowed the citizen suit, found violations after trial, imposed $405,800, and denied equitable relief.
FOE appealed the penalty amount; the Fourth Circuit vacated and directed dismissal as moot.
The Supreme Court reversed and remanded on January 12, 2000, leaving factual mootness and other reserved questions for further proceedings.
limits: This narrative follows the canonical historical source brief, without a new opinion audit. Ecological harm was not demonstrated, and the majority instead identified injury to members’ uses and interests. Compliance, closure, diligent prosecution, fees, and Article II issues were not finally resolved. The assigned notes lack printed page 1228; Stevens and Kennedy wrote separate solo concurrences despite an erroneous textbook bracket.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Laidlaw’s discharges affect how members use the river
sections.cue: What were the permit violations, and what injury did the members describe?
paragraphs: Laidlaw operated a wastewater-treatment facility in Roebuck, South Carolina, discharging into the North Tyger River under a National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System permit effective January 1, 1987. The permit limited pollutants including mercury. Laidlaw exceeded mercury limits and violated monitoring and reporting requirements.

Members of Friends of the Earth and the other citizen organizations described specific nearby places where they had swum, fished, picnicked, watched birds, or otherwise enjoyed the river. Concern about Laidlaw’s discharges caused them to curtail those activities; some also described diminished property value or enjoyment. Their claimed injury concerned concrete uses and interests, not an abstract desire to enforce environmental law.

The district court eventually found no demonstrated environmental harm from the violations. That finding must remain separate from the members’ allegations and from the Supreme Court’s later conclusion that reasonable concerns about ongoing illegal discharges injured the members’ recreational, aesthetic and economic interests.

sections.title: Notice prompts a state settlement, followed by the citizen complaint
sections.cue: Why did the state lawsuit not end the litigation at the district-court stage?
paragraphs: On April 10, 1992, Friends of the Earth gave the required sixty-day notice of intent to sue. Laidlaw then asked South Carolina’s Department of Health and Environmental Control to sue it. The district court later found that Laidlaw sought that action to preclude the citizen suit. DHEC and Laidlaw settled for $100,000 on June 9, before the notice period expired.

FOE filed the citizen complaint on June 12, alleging ongoing permit violations and seeking declaratory and injunctive relief and civil penalties payable to the United States. Citizens Local Environmental Action Network participated, and Sierra Club later joined. The district court rejected Laidlaw’s standing defense and determined that the state had not diligently prosecuted, allowing the citizen case to proceed. The Supreme Court did not finally decide that separate statutory defense. Laidlaw’s assistance in initiating the state suit was relevant evidence, not a rule that every defendant-assisted state action necessarily fails the diligent-prosecution requirement.

sources.pinpoint: Parties and Material Facts; Procedural History; Complete original-opinion clarifications; 528 U.S. 176–178, 211 n.4

sections.title: Trial produces a penalty but no injunction
sections.cue: What did the district court find, and what did FOE actually appeal?
paragraphs: After trial, the district court found 489 mercury-limit violations between 1987 and 1995, including thirteen after the citizen complaint, along with thirteen monitoring and ten reporting violations during the identified period. The last recorded mercury violation occurred in January 1995. The court’s references to substantial compliance since August 1992 did not mean that Laidlaw had complied perfectly throughout.

On January 22, 1997, the district court found an economic benefit from noncompliance of $1,092,581 and imposed a $405,800 penalty after considering the statutory factors and total deterrent effect. It denied declaratory and injunctive relief because of substantial compliance. The judgment anticipated possible attorneys’ fees but awarded none; the fee-petition deadline was stayed pending appeal.

FOE appealed the penalty amount, not the denial of equitable relief. The Fourth Circuit assumed standing at filing but held the remaining penalty claim moot because money payable to the Treasury could not redress private injury. It vacated and ordered dismissal. Laidlaw closed the facility after that appellate decision. The Supreme Court therefore confronted both whether FOE had penalty standing initially and whether later events had eliminated the controversy.

sources.pinpoint: Procedural History; Complete original-opinion clarifications; 528 U.S. 178–180, 193–195

sections.title: The Supreme Court connects the members’ losses to deterrence
sections.cue: How could payment to the government redress these plaintiffs’ injuries?
paragraphs: Justice Ginsburg wrote for Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justices Stevens, O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter and Breyer. The majority required concrete injury, causation and likely redressability and required standing separately for each remedy. It did not derive penalty standing automatically from standing to request an injunction.

The members described particular activities at identified places curtailed because of reasonable concerns tied to concededly ongoing illegal discharges. That differed from Lujan’s indefinite someday travel plans or conclusory use of unspecified areas. Requiring additional proof of actual ecological damage would make standing more demanding than proving some Clean Water Act violations on the merits. The majority did not find proven mercury damage to the ecosystem or announce that any unsupported subjective fear establishes injury.

A substantial civil penalty could deter future violations by making noncompliance less profitable, thereby reducing the threat that kept these members away from the river. A remedy can redress injury without transferring money to the plaintiff. Steel Co. involved wholly past violations; Laidlaw’s violations were ongoing when the complaint was filed. The Court recognized that deterrence might sometimes be too remote or insubstantial, but did not define those outer limits.

In answering the structural objection, the majority distinguished Linda R. S. and noted federal participation and support, including the Department of Justice and EPA. Those observations did not decide the reserved Article II question about private pursuit of public penalties. The inadequacy of the state settlement to deter or remove the economic benefit also remained part of the Court’s discussion, rather than a substitute for proof of these members’ interests.

sections.title: Later compliance raises a different burden
sections.cue: Why did denial of an injunction and closure not automatically require dismissal?
paragraphs: Standing asks whether a plaintiff met Article III requirements when suit began. Mootness asks whether later developments removed a live controversy. The majority rejected simply equating the two inquiries. Plaintiffs bear the initial standing burden, while a defendant relying on its voluntary cessation must make it absolutely clear that the challenged conduct cannot reasonably be expected to recur. Otherwise a defendant could stop during litigation and resume after dismissal.

Substantial compliance could moot this case if Laidlaw met that formidable burden, but the Supreme Court did not find that question conclusively resolved. Denying an injunction did not establish that no future violation remained for a penalty to deter: an injunction might be excessively intrusive where penalties provided sufficient deterrence. Closure also required factual consideration. It occurred after the Fourth Circuit ruling, and Laidlaw retained its permit. The record did not permit a final determination of recurrence.

The majority’s discussion of sunk costs concerned costs already incurred by the judicial system, not a party’s wish to recoup expenses. It did not authorize courts to retain cases after the parties plainly lost a continuing interest. It also explained that even subsequent mootness would not necessarily require vacating a district judgment when the losing party’s voluntary act caused the mootness.

The Court reversed the Fourth Circuit and remanded on January 12, 2000. It did not conclusively resolve compliance or closure, or reinstate an unalterable penalty. No fee award or denial was before it, so costs and fees belonged first in the district court. The Court expressly left the catalyst theory undecided.

sections.title: The separate opinions identify the remaining disagreements
sections.cue: Distinguish the two solo concurrences from Scalia and Thomas’s dissent.
paragraphs: Justice Stevens concurred alone. He would treat the civil-penalty claim as surviving voluntary compliance after filing even if compliance preceded judgment and made prospective relief moot. He compared penalties to punitive damages and emphasized that later events should not retroactively invalidate a valid monetary judgment. That reasoning went beyond the majority’s decision to leave the compliance and closure questions open.

Justice Kennedy also concurred alone. He reserved difficult Article II questions about private recovery of public fines and delegation of executive power. The certiorari petition, lower-court treatment and briefing had not specifically developed them. An assigned-text bracket incorrectly depicts Kennedy as joining Stevens; the original participation statement and opinion headings identify two separate solo concurrences.

Justice Scalia, joined by Justice Thomas, objected to injury, redressability, and the majority’s larger standing/mootness distinction. Given the trial finding of no demonstrated environmental harm, he regarded the members’ subjective concerns and testimony as insufficient without an objectively demonstrable threat. On redressability he distinguished the general availability of penalties from the marginal deterrent effect of an additional penalty in this case. General deterrence, he argued, did not establish sufficiently particularized and likely redress of these plaintiffs’ injuries and weakened Steel Co. and Article III limits. He discussed executive control but declined to decide the unargued Article II issue.

Assuming initial penalty standing, which he rejected, Scalia agreed that remand of the fact-sensitive voluntary-cessation question was sensible. He understood the ordinary cessation rule as an evidentiary presumption within a continuing controversy, not a relaxation of Article III. His notes preserved diligent prosecution, rejected Stevens’s damages analogy because Treasury penalties do not compensate the plaintiff, and examined possible descriptions of the Fourth Circuit’s ruling. His objections to governmental intervention and one administration’s acquiescence were dissenting arguments.

The assigned notes’ capable-of-repetition discussion supplies a comparison, not the majority’s basis; this case used voluntary cessation. Printed page 1228 is missing, so the full first note cannot be reconstructed. The available later discussion of West Virginia v. EPA is editorial context. The complete second note attributes to Daniel Farber a place-based standing proposal combining Laidlaw and Massachusetts v. EPA; the Court did not adopt that scholarly proposal here.
